The cloak compresses space from a cylindrical region of radius a = 27.1 mm into an annular shell extending to radius b = 58.9 mm.
Material parameters include constant permittivity ε_z = 3.423 and permeability μ_θ = 1, with radially varying μ_r.
The metamaterial consists of 10 concentric cylindrical layers, each three unit cells tall, with split ring resonators oriented radially.
The unit cell dimensions are a_θ = a_z = 10/3 mm, with SRR rings of 3 mm square size and 0.2 mm width on a 381 μm thick Duroid 5870 substrate.
Microwaves in the 8-12 GHz X-band are introduced into a parallel-plate waveguide with 11 mm plate spacing for measurements.
The cloak reduces both backscatter and forward scattering (shadow) from a copper cylinder concealed inside it.
The optimal operating frequency of the cloak is experimentally confirmed at 8.5 GHz, matching simulation predictions.
The cloak's electromagnetic parameters are anisotropic and spatially varying, requiring complex metamaterial design.
The split ring resonators are alternated in orientation to minimize magnetoelectric coupling.
The metamaterial unit cells are modeled as right rectangular prisms in simulations despite their curved sector geometry in the actual cloak.
The cloak demonstrates the first practical realization of transformation optics-based electromagnetic cloaking at microwave frequencies.
Full two-dimensional spatial field maps of amplitude and phase were acquired experimentally to validate the cloak's performance.
The wavefront inside the cloak exhibits compression and intensity reduction near the inner radius before reforming on the opposite side.
Material absorption and parameter approximations limit the cloak's performance and bandwidth.
The cloak design relies on the form invariance of Maxwell’s equations under coordinate transformations.
The metamaterial cloak is fabricated using hundreds of SRRs arranged in a non-cubic, cylindrical lattice.
The experimental apparatus allows precise scanning of the field by moving the lower plate relative to a fixed antenna.
The cloak effectively makes the combined object and cloak appear electromagnetically equivalent to free space externally.
The cloak's design and measurements confirm the feasibility of implementing complex anisotropic media with metamaterials.
The research opens new pathways for controlling electromagnetic fields using transformation optics.
